Living in space is really more about what you can make there than what you might find there. If we're talking about real places in space, aside from the views of the stars, maybe a majestic view of a nearby Saturn or Jupiter, or some interesting landscape, most every place in the solar system other than Earth is rather similar. They're all pretty-much Iceland/Greenland/Atacama Desert with different gravity. Beautiful in their own right, certainly, but there's not a hell of a lot going on during the weekend. The most unusual environments might be the under-ice oceans of Saturn's Enceladus and Jupiter's Europa and Ganymede. But those are also mostly lightless environments, so you might not be able to see anything at all. I could take any of them. Other than Earth, there's not that much difference.

So what really makes any particular place in space interesting as a place to live is how you go about making it habitable, adapting its environment to suit you or adapting yourself to suit it, and the culture and architecture that results from that. Unless a planet is already very close in characteristics to Earth, making it casually surface-habitable like Earth is rather difficult. Only Mars and Venus offer us this prospect in our solar system and would require some radical and colossal engineering to pull-off. We very often hear talk about terraforming Mars, but what's overlooked is that Mars has no active geology anymore and so no significant magnetosphere to protect its atmosphere from being stripped away by solar winds. So, even if you managed to terraform it, it won't keep. You'll have to constantly restore that atmosphere by artificial means. This is wasteful and so you would ideally want to engineer some kind of artificial magnetosphere. Burrow into the planet's core and make some gigantic field coil powered--somehow--using radioactive materials you can find in the planet or supply from elsewhere. That's not especially likely.

Venus has a much harsher environment because of its runaway greenhouse effect, but it might be a somewhat easier problem to deal with--as titanic engineering projects go... You would need to bring one or more asteroids into Venus' orbit and convert them into one or more enormous solar shades, and likely solar power collectors too. Then you could cool the planet enough to possibly terraform it. You might have to wait many centuries, though, before it cools enough to begin. Recently people have been talking of the possibility of limiting the settlement of Venus to its much less harsh and rather Earth-like upper atmosphere, using large aerostat structures and airships. However, exploiting the local resources to make such habitats when the surface can still destroy the most hardened machines in minutes to hours remains something of a challenge.

Given the known technology for building habitats, most of the natural environments of the solar system leave us with only one practical option; going underground or building massive masonry structures that are largely the same as being underground. That means you're living indoors 99.99% of the time. Forget the giant transparent domes of old SciFi or conventional windows of any sort. Your outdoor views will be by video windows and natural lighting will be piped in--which may not be so bad as light field imaging systems and large flexible displays will soon approach the quality of conventional windows at far less cost for space use. Near-future spacecraft may soon obsolesce windows with virtual windows, and gain very large viewing areas as a result.

So if you want to know what living in space is most-likely to look like, here it is. This is the Kansas City Subtropolis; a light industrial campus built into a limestone mine. Almost everywhere in the solar system, this is pretty much what we're going to get. The chief differences from this are basically scale. In lower gravity you can use much larger spans and arch and dome spaces are likely. In microgravity, as with asteroids, they might use spherical and cylindrical spaces with spaceframes to mount things and help get you around. This doesn't seem so bad to me. If it weren't for the trucks, I'd live in the Subtropolis. The question is, starting with spaces like this, how would you make a comfortable and fun place to live? There are a lot of possibilities. The peculiarly named Grin Grin Park in Japan offers us a glimpse at one approach. This structure is built using a method very likely to be used in space; mound formed concrete, noted for its use by German military engineers in building bomb resistant aircraft hangars during WWII. You cast your footings and floor then pile-up gravel into mounds and sculpt them into the shape of your building. You put rebar into the surface of the gravel and pour concrete over the mounds to make a reinforced shell structure. You them 'berm' that with earth and landscape it. When the shell is hardened, you dig out the gravel leaving your rigid man-made cave and reuse it to build your next structures. In space you wouldn't often see the outside surface of such structures, and the skylights would be fiber optic light emitters and lamps, but you could have the same free-form spaces at truly vast scales.

It's often suggested that, because of the limits in adapting natural bodies in space to an Earth-like environment, the use of giant rotating orbital colonies is more likely for general space habitation. The problem with that idea is that this grandiose engineering solution to the problem of 'space wasting' is in competition with clinical solutions--ways of adapting the human body itself. That may arrive by the time we have the technical capability to make such habitats and will always be more cost-effective, obsolescing any more expensive options as soon as they turn-up. So the more likely form of orbital human habitat will be progressively bigger versions of the TransHab or Bigelow habitat. Imagine that as big as a skyscraper, which is pretty-much the same thing from an indoor perspective as a small asteroid habitat.

This brings up the even bigger issue of whether there is a place for organic human life in space at all if space is, in fact, a competition for cost-efficiency. The only economically practical reason for people to be in space--the only 'paying job'--is as a solution to telecommunications latency. To be a mind controlling telerobots. Forget space suits and EVAs. That's not in the cards. Humans aren't doing the heavy lifting out there. So it's a question of whether we run machines from offices on Earth, from shirt-sleeve habitats closer by, or we can let the machines run themselves. This means that the window of opportunity for us organic humans to get our act together and setup sustainable settlements in space is from this moment right now to whenever we get Artificial General Intelligence--which most futurists today think may be 30 years or less away. Once we have that, it becomes the cheaper solution to the latency problem. And it doesn't have to have parity with human intelligence. It just needs to be smart enough to replace teleoperation with executive management--and then we're back on Earth sitting in offices waiting for reports. The fastest, most cost-effective, and most convenient way to travel in space is by telecommunications. The mind that can travel by that means is the mind that rules space. If you think there is any possibility that artilects will exist in the near future, our role in space is over. We will either have to figure out how to join the artilects, as a way of adapting ourselves to living out there, or we'll be tourists at their convenience.

So it's possible that the most likely kind of habitat suited to the most places in space is a data center hosting a virtual reality habitat for communities of artilects. In that habitat the artilect can create any sort of home they wish, without regard to the external environment. They will work in that external environment by telepresence and executive management of non-sentient AIs. They will travel across space as casually as we would step through a door into our back yard. This may be the most likely vision of life in space. Yet it's a vision no one is showing us today. Not space agencies, not space advocacy, not even Science Fiction. It doesn't seem heroic enough. It remains too hard for us to imagine artilects as us and VR environments as just as real as our mostly artificial houses and buildings. The notion of giving up our bodies to live in space seems too creepy. Hollywood is always portraying the artilect as monster, alien, or Pinocchio rather than simply people. I think the scariest thing about AI for people today is the possibility that it might turn out just like us.
